message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact bandwidth you’re getting right now.  
But you can find out quickly yourself—either with a web‑based speed test or by running a small command‑line test on your own machine.

---

## 1. Web‑based speed tests (easiest)

| Site | How to use |
|------|------------|
| **Speedtest by Ookla** | Visit <https://www.speedtest.net> and click “Go”. |
| **Fast.com** | Visit <https://fast.com> – it starts measuring automatically. |
| **Google Speed Test** | Search “internet speed test” on Google; the built‑in widget will start automatically. |

These services will report:

* **Download speed** (Mbps)
* **Upload speed** (Mbps)
* **Ping / latency** (ms)

---

## 2. Command‑line speed tests

If you prefer a terminal/PowerShell approach, you can use the official `speedtest-cli` tool.

### Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
# 1. Install the tool (requires PowerShell 5+)
Install-Module -Name SpeedTest -Scope CurrentUser -Force

# 2. Run a test
Invoke-SpeedTest
```

### Linux/macOS (bash)

```bash
# Install via pip (Python package)
pip install speedtest-cli

# Run the test
speedtest-cli
```

### Using `curl` or `wget` (quick & dirty)

If you just want a rough idea of download speed, you can download a known‑size file and time it:

```powershell
# PowerShell example (Windows)
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$start = Get-Date
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile "$env:TEMP\testfile.bin"
$end = Get-Date
$elapsed = ($end - $start).TotalSeconds
$bytes = (Get-Item "$env:TEMP\testfile.bin").Length
$mbps = ($bytes / 1_000_000) / $elapsed * 8
Write-Host "Approx. download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) Mbps"
```

> **Tip:** Replace the URL with a file hosted on a server close to you for a more accurate measurement.

---

## 3. Quick sanity check in Windows without installing anything

If you just want a quick sanity check, you can use the built‑in `netsh` command to see current link speed:

```powershell
netsh interface ipv4 show subinterfaces
```

Look for the “Link speed” column. This shows the *maximum* speed your NIC reports to the OS (e.g., 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps), not the actual throughput you’re experiencing.

---

## 4. What to look for

| Metric | What it means | Typical values |
|--------|---------------|----------------|
| **Download speed** | How fast data comes into your device | 10–100 Mbps for home broadband, 1–10 Gbps for fiber |
| **Upload speed** | How fast data leaves your device | Usually lower than download; 1–10 Mbps for home |
| **Latency (ping)** | Round‑trip time to a server | < 20 ms for gaming, < 50 ms for streaming |

---

### Bottom line

- **Use a web site** if you just want a quick readout.
- **Use `speedtest-cli`** if you prefer a terminal or want to script it.
- **Use `netsh`** to see the NIC’s advertised link speed.

Let me know if you’d like help installing `speedtest-cli`, or if you’re on a different OS and need tailored instructions!
